reading.body:
Healthcare AI vendors face overlapping regulatory burdens across data privacy, liability, and cross-border governance that create distinct operational friction points absent from consumer AI.

The tools listed span clinical decision support, medical language models, drug discovery, and genomic analysis. Each operates under different compliance frameworks. US-based clinical tools must navigate HIPAA, FDA software as a medical device rules, and diagnostic liability. Google's medical LLM requires business associate agreements and carries explicit liability exposure. Tempus handles genetic data under GINA constraints. Insilico Medicine, operating from Hong Kong, operates under different jurisdictional regimes entirely while handling sensitive molecular and clinical data that can flow across borders.

This fragmentation matters for AI infrastructure because healthcare AI cannot simply scale like consumer models. A clinical decision support system deployed in one health system cannot be trivially moved or retrained without re-certification. Data residency and HIPAA business associate requirements constrain where computation can occur and who can access training data. Drug discovery AI like Insilico's must balance IP generation across jurisdictions with data provenance tracking. These are not compute problems; they are governance problems that precede compute allocation.

The data covers vendor tooling and regulatory surface but does not address infrastructure requirements, power consumption, or the actual building footprints required to host these systems in compliant jurisdictions. It also does not show which tools actually run at scale in production versus research stage, or how frequently regulatory changes force retraining or redeployment cycles that consume additional compute.
